method: One text is quoted for the shell. The single-quoted form wraps it in single quotes and writes each embedded single quote as a close quote, a backslash-escaped quote and a reopened quote, because a single quote cannot appear between single quotes; an empty text becomes two single quotes and still does not count as a bare word. The bare form is offered only when every character is in the set A-Z a-z 0-9 _ @ % + = : , . / -, which the shell reads literally. The double-quoted form is offered for one-line text without control characters and escapes the dollar sign, the backquote, the double quote and the backslash, which POSIX keeps special between double quotes, while a backslash before any other character is left as it is. The ANSI-C form is offered when the text holds control characters and writes them as \a \b \t \n \v \f \r \E or \xHH, escaping the backslash and the single quote, a form bash, ksh93 and zsh understand and POSIX sh does not. Every form is read back with the page's own quote-removal rules - single quotes keep every character, double quotes drop a backslash only before $ ` " \ or a newline, an unquoted backslash protects the next character, and $'...' decodes named, octal, \xHH, \uHHHH and \UHHHHHHHH escapes - and each must reproduce the text exactly. Each extra nesting layer quotes the previous line again for an outer sh -c, su or ssh. Decode mode runs the same rules on one word, reports the quote styles it used and the canonical single-quoted form of the result, refuses an unquoted space, tab or newline, an unterminated quote and a trailing unquoted backslash, and warns when an unquoted dollar sign, backquote, glob character, tilde, exclamation mark, brace or control operator means a real shell would expand the word or read it as more than one command. Lengths are counted in code points and UTF-8 bytes. Text holding a NUL byte is refused because a shell word cannot carry one, and the text is limited to 8192 characters on the page.

sources.title: POSIX.1-2017 Shell Command Language, 2.2 Quoting: single quotes preserve the literal value of each character and a single quote cannot appear between them, while double quotes preserve every character except the dollar sign, the backquote and the backslash, which keeps its escape meaning only before $, `, ", \ or a newline.

bash(1) QUOTING: four quoting mechanisms - the escape character, single quotes, double quotes and $'...' dollar-single quotes - where ANSI-C escapes such as \a, \n, \xHH and \uHHHH are decoded, ! stays special between double quotes while history expansion is enabled, and a backslash before any other character inside double quotes is left unmodified.
